question: Which phase of the menstrual cycle comes immediately after ovulation?

options.A: The luteal phase
options.B: The menstrual phase
options.C: The proliferative phase
options.D: The follicular phase

explanation: Right after ovulation, the cycle enters the luteal phase. This is when the leftover follicle forms the corpus luteum to produce progesterone.

question: What does the ruptured follicle turn into after ovulation occurs?

options.A: Corpus luteum
options.B: Endometrial polyp
options.C: Primordial cyst
options.D: Graafian follicle

explanation: The leftover follicular cells change structurally and functionally to become the hormone-secreting corpus luteum. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T3#GNS216_U2_T3_h5)

question: Why is teaching workers about toxic gases important in factories and industrial sites?

options.A: It helps workers recognize hidden breathing hazards and use safety gear
options.B: It eliminates the need for any medical staff on site
options.C: It reduces the cost of electricity in factories
options.D: It guarantees that machinery will never break down

explanation: Many toxic gases are invisible. Educating workers helps them spot dangers early and protect themselves with proper ventilation and masks.

question: Why is the Plate Method often recommended over strict food weighing for beginners?

options.A: It offers a simple visual guide that is easy to remember and use daily.
options.B: It eliminates the need to ever eat carbohydrates again.
options.C: It guarantees that blood sugar levels will never fluctuate above normal.
options.D: It is the only medically approved method for type 1 diabetes.

explanation: Visual portion guides reduce the intimidation of meal planning and make healthy eating sustainable in everyday life. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T012#GNS227_U6_T012_h4)

question: What makes inhaled medications act so much faster than oral medications?

options.A: The massive surface area and rich blood supply of the lungs
options.B: The protective mucus lining that rapidly dissolves all capsules
options.C: The direct passage of drugs through the thick stomach wall
options.D: The strong muscular contractions found inside the bronchioles

explanation: The large surface area and extensive capillary network in the lungs allow rapid absorption directly into the bloodstream without first passing through the digestive system. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T19#GNS125_U3_T19_h1)

question: Why does the fertile window include the days *before* ovulation, and not just the day of release?

options.A: Intercourse must happen early to trigger the LH surge.
options.B: Hormones take several days to travel from the brain to the ovaries.
options.C: Sperm can survive in the female reproductive tract for up to five days.
options.D: Eggs can live inside the fallopian tube for nearly a week.

explanation: Sperm are troopers! They can hang out and stay fertile inside the female tract for up to 5 days, waiting for the egg to arrive.

question: How does the high humidity inside a steam tent help a patient with a heavy cough?

options.A: It dilates the tiny air sacs in the lower lungs
options.B: It kills bacterial infections in the upper airway
options.C: It numbs the throat nerves to stop the cough reflex
options.D: It liquefies thick mucus so it is easier to clear

explanation: Spot on! Moisture acts like magic on sticky mucus, thinning it out so the patient can cough it up easily.

question: Which board must review and approve any research involving human participants before data collection starts?

options.A: Institutional Review Board
options.B: Hospital Maintenance Committee
options.C: Financial Audit Committee
options.D: Nursing Licensing Board

explanation: The IRB acts as a safety shield, checking research plans to protect human participants from harm.

question: What is the main job of the immune system in the human body?

options.A: Pumping oxygen-rich blood throughout body tissues
options.B: Breaking down food nutrients for energy production
options.C: Regulating hormone levels in the bloodstream
options.D: Defending the body against foreign invaders and abnormal cells

explanation: Think of your immune system as your body's security guard! Its main job is to protect you from harmful germs like bacteria and viruses, as well as keeping internal threats in check.

question: A patient is admitted with a skin infection spread by direct touch. Which nursing action is most important?

options.A: Placing the patient in a negative pressure isolation room
options.B: Putting on gloves and a gown before touching the patient's skin
options.C: Spraying the hallway air with strong chemical disinfectants
options.D: Boiling all eating utensils before the patient uses them

explanation: Because direct contact involves skin-to-skin touch or touching infected lesions, barriers like gloves and gowns block the transfer of pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h3)

question: Why do community health nurses love using the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) tape in the field?

options.A: It is quick, easy to use, and does not require complex scales
options.B: It is the only tool that can accurately measure linear height in toddlers
options.C: It gives an exact measurement of the child's total body fat percentage
options.D: It replaces the need to check for clinical signs of vitamin deficiency

explanation: Exactly! MUAC is portable, fast, and practical when you are out in community outreaches screening lots of children quickly.

question: Why do we grab a cold pack immediately after someone suffers a fresh joint sprain?

options.A: To heat up the deep tissue and relax tight tendons
options.B: To stimulate rapid cell division in the bone
options.C: To dilate vessels and increase local bleeding
options.D: To constrict blood vessels and reduce swelling

explanation: Spot on! Cold causes vasoconstriction (narrowing the vessels), which slows down blood flow to the fresh injury so it doesn't blow up into a huge swelling.

question: Why is regular self-reflection important for nurses working in post-abortion care?

options.A: It guarantees promotion to senior nursing administrative positions
options.B: It replaces the need for formal clinical pharmacology training
options.C: It helps nurses recognize their personal biases and prevent them from affecting care
options.D: It ensures the nurse never experiences physical fatigue on duty

explanation: Checking in with our own feelings helps us separate personal beliefs from professional duty, keeping our care fair and respectful.

question: What is the primary goal of performing a neurological examination?

options.A: To determine the exact blood type of the patient
options.B: To measure the patient's daily caloric intake
options.C: To diagnose specific psychiatric disorders
options.D: To evaluate the function of the nervous system

explanation: The neurological exam is specifically designed to assess how well the central and peripheral nervous systems are working. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h1)

question: What is the physical shape of a DNA molecule?

options.A: A flat square sheet
options.B: A single circle
options.C: A branched tree structure
options.D: A double helix

explanation: DNA naturally twists into a spiral ladder shape referred to as a double helix. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h1)

question: How does a negative feedback loop usually react when hormone levels drop too low?

options.A: It signals the endocrine glands to increase hormone production
options.B: It converts stored anabolism into rapid tissue breakdown
options.C: It forces the kidneys to excrete remaining electrolytes
options.D: It shuts down the pituitary gland completely to conserve energy

explanation: Negative feedback works just like an air conditioner thermostat. When levels drop, the body notices and tells the glands to pump out more hormone until balance is restored!

question: How do nitrogenous waste products like urea and creatinine cross from the fetus to the mother?

options.A: Simple diffusion
options.B: Active transport
options.C: Pinocytosis
options.D: Filtration via the fetal kidneys

explanation: Waste products move passively from areas of higher concentration in the fetus to lower concentration in maternal blood via simple diffusion. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T7#GNS121_U6_T7_h6)

question: Which atom in the human body is primarily targeted during an MRI scan?

options.A: Hydrogen
options.B: Sodium
options.C: Calcium
options.D: Carbon

explanation: Because the body has so much water, hydrogen protons are abundant and react strongly to the MRI magnetic field. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T12#GNS123_U2_T12_h2)

question: What is the safest way to handle a used injection needle?

options.A: Break the needle off the syringe by hand
options.B: Drop it immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container
options.C: Recap it firmly using both hands before walking away
options.D: Place it inside a regular plastic waste bin

explanation: You've got it! Never mess around with used needles. Drop them straight into the sharps box to avoid accidental pricks.

question: Which of the following describes the difference between macronutrients and micronutrients?

options.A: Micronutrients are digested much faster than any macronutrient
options.B: Micronutrients are needed in smaller amounts and do not provide direct calories
options.C: Macronutrients are stored in bones while micronutrients float in blood
options.D: Macronutrients are only needed during childhood and growth phases

explanation: While macronutrients are consumed in large amounts for energy and structure, micronutrients are needed in tiny amounts to regulate body processes without supplying calories. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h3)

question: Which two major organs take the heaviest hit from long-term, uncontrolled high blood pressure?

options.A: Liver and pancreas
options.B: Heart and kidneys
options.C: Lungs and stomach
options.D: Spleen and thyroid

explanation: Because the heart and kidneys are packed with delicate blood vessels, they bear the brunt of constant high pressure, leading to heart and kidney failure over time.

question: What main trigger causes the kidneys to release erythropoietin in patients with chronic lung disease?

options.A: High levels of red blood cells in circulation
options.B: Increased blood pressure in the right atrium
options.C: Persistent low blood oxygen levels
options.D: Reduced production of pulmonary surfactant

explanation: Brilliant! When the kidneys sense low oxygen (hypoxemia) over a long time, they release erythropoietin to tell the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h7)

question: What is a major goal of physical therapy in the long-term management of a child with spastic cerebral palsy?

options.A: Eliminating the need for any assistive devices by age five
options.B: Preventing joint contractures and improving functional mobility
options.C: Permanently stopping all involuntary muscle contractions
options.D: Curing the underlying brain lesion through intense exercise

explanation: Physical therapy uses stretching, strengthening, and positioning to keep muscles pliable and prevent permanent joint tightening. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h6)

question: Which routine nursing task calls for clean examination gloves?

options.A: Measuring a patient's resting blood pressure
options.B: Handing a clean meal tray to a patient
options.C: Adjusting nasal cannula oxygen flow
options.D: Emptying a urinary catheter drainage bag

explanation: Urine is a body fluid, so you definitely want glove protection to avoid exposure when emptying that drainage bag. Simple and safe!

question: What is a major complication if an intramuscular injection is given incorrectly in the buttocks?

options.A: Sudden elevation of intraocular pressure
options.B: Sciatic nerve injury leading to pain or paralysis
options.C: Immediate development of systemic respiratory failure
options.D: Complete blockage of the carotid artery

explanation: The sciatic nerve runs right through the lower, inner part of the buttock. This is why proper site landmarks (like the upper outer quadrant) are so crucial!

question: How can a severe shortage of nurses lead to unsafe injections?

options.A: It gives nurses extra time to clean equipment
options.B: It automatically gets rid of multi-dose vials
options.C: It causes rushed procedures where safety steps get skipped
options.D: It forces patients to inject themselves

explanation: When you're overworked and tired, it's easy to rush. Staying aware helps us protect our patients even on busy shifts.

question: Why are bedside nurses considered the frontline defenders in clinical risk management?

options.A: They decide which doctors get suspended for errors.
options.B: They handle all legal lawsuits filed by patients.
options.C: They observe daily workflows and spot hazards firsthand.
options.D: They write the official hospital policies and budget plans.

explanation: Bedside nurses work directly with patients every day, placing them in the best position to notice subtle workflow issues and safety risks. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T9#GNS312_U5_T9_h1)

question: When giving ear drops to an adult, how should you pull the ear pinna?

options.A: Downward and forward
options.B: Downward and backward
options.C: Straight outward
options.D: Upward and backward

explanation: Great clinical technique! For adults, pulling the pinna upward and backward straightens out that curvy ear canal so your drops flow smoothly down to the eardrum.

question: A hospital ward manager reads a newly published study proving a new dressing reduces infection rates. What action represents utilizing this research?

options.A: Scolding staff nurses for not discovering the dressing themselves
options.B: Filing the journal away in a drawer for future decoration
options.C: Ignoring the study because the old dressing is cheaper to buy
options.D: Updating the ward's wound care policy to adopt the new dressing

explanation: Utilizing research means putting proven evidence-based changes into active clinical practice. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why is the gut often called our second brain regarding mood?

options.A: It prevents all forms of physical inflammation
options.B: It directly digests complex psychiatric medications
options.C: It completely replaces the function of the brain
options.D: It produces most of the body's serotonin supply

explanation: Correct! Specialized cells and microbes in your gut manufacture a large share of your body's serotonin, directly influencing your mood.

question: Into what smaller forms must dietary proteins be broken down before they can be absorbed?

options.A: Complex polysaccharides
options.B: Amino acids and small peptides
options.C: Emulsified fat globules
options.D: Whole polypeptide chains

explanation: Proteins are usually too bulky to pass through the gut wall as they are, so digestive enzymes break them down into tiny building blocks like amino acids first.

question: What is assisted partner notification in HIV care?

options.A: A service where healthcare providers help notify sexual partners safely with client consent
options.B: An automated text message sent to every citizen in the country
options.C: A public radio broadcast listing the names of newly diagnosed patients
options.D: A police-enforced arrest warrant for individuals who test positive

explanation: Assisted notification steps in to bridge the gap when a client cannot safely disclose to their partner alone. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h6)

question: Why are iodine solutions sometimes given before a thyroid surgery?

options.A: To decrease the size and blood supply of the thyroid gland
options.B: To permanently cure the underlying autoimmune disease process
options.C: To permanently destroy excess thyroid tissue without surgery
options.D: To prevent the development of postoperative hypocalcemia

explanation: You got it! Preoperative iodine shrinks the gland and cuts down its blood vessels, making the surgery much safer with less bleeding.

question: A patient touches a hot stove and quickly pulls their hand away. Which receptors flagged this danger?

options.A: Proprioceptors and mechanoreceptors
options.B: Baroreceptors and chemoreceptors
options.C: Photoreceptors and osmoreceptors
options.D: Thermoreceptors and nociceptors

explanation: Brilliant! Thermoreceptors felt the intense heat, and nociceptors screamed 'ouch!'—triggering that fast reflex to protect the hand.

question: Why can unsafe formula feeding sometimes pose an even greater danger to an infant than HIV?

options.A: Contaminated water and dirty bottles cause fatal diarrhea and severe malnutrition
options.B: Commercial formula lacks basic calories needed for normal brain growth
options.C: Babies fed with formula develop immediate resistance to routine vaccines
options.D: Prepared formula breaks down the infant immune system faster than the virus

explanation: Where clean water isn't guaranteed, bad hygiene around formula bottles can cause severe tummy bugs that put a baby's life at serious risk.

question: Why must a nursing school periodically evaluate its instructional materials?

options.A: To ensure they still reflect current clinical guidelines and practice
options.B: To reduce the number of teachers needed in the department
options.C: To make the storage room look more organized
options.D: To comply with school building construction codes

explanation: Nursing practice changes rapidly, so teaching resources must be evaluated regularly to ensure they do not teach outdated or unsafe methods. [learn more](GST321_U8_T4#GST321_U8_T4_h7)

question: A patient with an injury to their supplementary motor area would have the hardest time doing which of these?

options.A: Playing a practiced song on the piano from memory
options.B: Seeing a bright flashing light across the hospital room
options.C: Reflexively pulling a hand away from a hot stove burner
options.D: Feeling the texture of a piece of smooth velvet fabric

explanation: Playing an instrument takes smoothly linked, sequential movements—which is right up the SMA's alley!

question: A young patient is scared that birth control pills cause permanent infertility because of community rumors. What is your best response?

options.A: Confirm her fears and suggest she never use any form of modern medicine
options.B: Provide calm, factual education explaining that fertility returns after stopping
options.C: Refuse to prescribe any medication until she agrees to stop asking questions
options.D: Scold the patient for listening to uneducated members of the community

explanation: You're a health educator! Always meet patient fears with patience and facts, reassuring them that fertility bounces back once they stop taking the pills.

question: What is a major economic headache for the long-term capital of a DRF?

options.A: High rates of national inflation eroding purchasing power
options.B: Strict adherence to quality assurance during procurement
options.C: An excessive surplus of cash sitting in the pharmacy safe
options.D: Too many patients buying generic drugs instead of brands

explanation: When inflation hits hard, prices shoot up. The same amount of cash buys fewer and fewer drugs over time, making it tough to keep shelves full.

question: Why is it so important to send a routine urine sample to the lab right away, or keep it in the fridge if there's a delay?

options.A: Prompt delivery prevents the patient from changing their mind about the test
options.B: Room temperature encourages bacterial growth and chemical breakdown
options.C: Leaving it out causes the plastic container to melt in warm rooms
options.D: Refrigeration speeds up the chemical reaction on dipstick pads

explanation: Urine left sitting in a warm room changes quickly—bacteria love to multiply in it, and cellular casts start to break apart, which ruins the accuracy of the test!

question: What is the primary medication class used as first-line treatment for minimal change disease?

options.A: Antivirals
options.B: Antibiotics
options.C: Corticosteroids
options.D: Beta blockers

explanation: Corticosteroids reduce inflammation and immune activity that damage the glomerular filter, making them the standard starting treatment. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h4)

question: What is another common medical name for hydatid disease?

options.A: Taeniasis
options.B: Schistosomiasis
options.C: Ascariasis
options.D: Echinococcosis

explanation: Hydatid disease comes from tapeworm larvae and is medically called echinococcosis. You've got this!

question: A patient with severe liver disease is at high risk for bleeding. Which nursing care step is best?

options.A: Instructing the patient to use an electric razor for shaving
options.B: Giving all routine medications through deep muscle injections
options.C: Encouraging daily flossing with stiff-bristled dental tools
options.D: Applying firm pressure bandages to all minor skin sites

explanation: An electric razor prevents nicks and cuts. Since a failing liver struggles with clotting, we want to avoid any accidental bleeding!

question: Which of these is an important warning sign you must teach a patient before they go home after a proctoscopy?

options.A: Normal resumption of eating food
options.B: Heavy or continuous rectal bleeding
options.C: Mild passing of gas for two hours
options.D: A temporary feeling of rectal fullness

explanation: Spot on! A tiny bit of spotting can happen, but heavy or ongoing bleeding is not normal. Always tell patients to report this right away.

question: When an endocrine gland responds to 'humoral' stimulation, what is it actually reacting to?

options.A: Direct commands from the cerebral cortex
options.B: Levels of nutrients and ions in the blood
options.C: Electrical signals from the spinal cord
options.D: The presence of circulating releasing factors

explanation: Great job remembering this! 'Humoral' just means the gland is tasting the blood for things like calcium or glucose and reacting to what it finds.

question: What is another name for the sympathetic division based on where its nerves leave the spinal cord?

options.A: Thoracolumbar division
options.B: Cervicothoracic division
options.C: Lumbosacral division
options.D: Craniosacral division

explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons emerge from the thoracic and upper lumbar regions of the spinal cord, giving it the thoracolumbar label. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T29#GNS211_U3_T29_h4)

question: What tough, fibrous layer of connective tissue tightly wraps around the corpora cavernosa to give it support?

options.A: Endothelial lining
options.B: Perineal membrane
options.C: Tunica albuginea
options.D: Trabecular fascia

explanation: You got this! The tunica albuginea is a strong, fibrous covering that acts like a supportive sleeve around the corpora cavernosa during an erection.

question: Which nursing action should you AVOID when trying to cool down a patient with a fever?

options.A: Giving prescribed paracetamol
options.B: Putting the patient in an ice-cold bath
options.C: Offering plenty of water to drink
options.D: Keeping the hospital room well-ventilated

explanation: Spot on! Ice-cold water makes the patient shiver violently, which actually pushes their internal temperature back up.

question: As a ward nurse handling hospital tools every day, what is your main responsibility regarding them?

options.A: Acting as primary custodian and daily operator
options.B: Purchasing replacement parts from suppliers
options.C: Designing and manufacturing new medical devices
options.D: Repairing all electrical faults on the ward

explanation: You use these tools right at the bedside every day, which means you are the key person making sure they are handled and checked properly!

question: What is the primary surgical goal of joint arthroplasty for a client with severe hip osteoarthritis?

options.A: Permanently fusing the hip bones together so they can never move again
options.B: Clearing out loose debris with a tiny camera without touching the bone
options.C: Cutting the thigh bone to shift body weight away from the damaged area
options.D: Replacing damaged bone and cartilage with artificial components to relieve pain

explanation: Arthroplasty involves total joint replacement where worn surfaces are swapped for artificial parts to restore pain-free movement. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T14#GNS222_U1_T14_h7)

question: Clinic records show few malaria cases, but local medicine vendors report selling lots of malaria drugs daily. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Report the clinic staff to the ministry for failing to do their jobs
options.B: Use community-based data collection like household surveys to find the real disease burden
options.C: Assume the medicine vendors are lying and close down their shops
options.D: Conclude that malaria has been completely eradicated in that area

explanation: Not everyone goes to the government clinic first; many buy drugs across the counter. To find the true picture, nurses must look beyond clinic logbooks and talk to the community directly.

question: Why are flashing lights and visual alert systems helpful for patients with severe hearing loss?

options.A: They provide visual warnings for home safety hazards that sounds might miss
options.B: Flashing lights help regenerate damaged hair cells inside the inner ear
options.C: They replace the need for regular hearing aid battery replacements
options.D: Bright lights automatically adjust the volume of household televisions

explanation: Brilliant! Since they might miss audio cues, flashing lights for doorbells or smoke alarms help keep them safe at home.

question: Imagine a sudden disease outbreak hits your ward and there is no existing hospital policy for it. What type of choice must you make?

options.A: Programmed choice
options.B: Strategic choice
options.C: Non-programmed choice
options.D: Routine choice

explanation: When a situation is totally new and unstructured, standard rules won't cut it. You have to make a non-programmed choice!

question: Which of these actions is a dangerous violation of medication safety rules?

options.A: Checking the expiry date on a drug vial prior to preparing the injection
options.B: Signing off that you gave a medication before the patient actually swallows it
options.C: Asking a patient to state their full name before handing them oral tablets
options.D: Verifying a calculated pediatric dose with a senior colleague

explanation: Spot on! Never sign for a drug before it's taken. Documenting care before it happens falsifies records and puts patients at risk.

question: A mum at 28 weeks comes to the clinic with swollen face and high blood pressure. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: The fetus is growing at an unusually rapid and healthy rate
options.B: The mother is simply eating too much salt in her daily diet
options.C: This is a completely normal physical change in the third trimester
options.D: These are potential warning signs of preeclampsia requiring prompt evaluation

explanation: You nailed it! Sudden facial swelling plus high BP are red flags for preeclampsia. We always check these out immediately to keep the mum safe.

question: What does a nurse typically see during an otoscopic exam of a patient with acute ear infection (otitis media)?

options.A: A clear, translucent eardrum with a sharp cone of light
options.B: A dark perforated hole with dry flaky skin inside the canal
options.C: A bulging, bright red tympanic membrane with obscured landmarks
options.D: A completely pale, flat membrane with prominent bone outlines

explanation: When pus builds up behind the eardrum from an infection, it pushes the drum outward and turns it very red, hiding the normal landmarks.

question: What is often the primary cure for a hormone-secreting endocrine tumor?

options.A: Complete removal of the liver and spleen
options.B: Lifelong high-dose antibiotic therapy
options.C: Drinking large amounts of plain water
options.D: Surgical removal of the tumor

explanation: When an overactive gland or tumor is causing hypersecretion, cutting it out is usually the fastest and most direct cure. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T7#GNS211_U1_T7_h5)

question: When is rabies post-exposure prophylaxis necessary after an animal bite?

options.A: Only if the human victim shows signs of neurological confusion
options.B: If the patient has not received a tetanus shot within the past year
options.C: When the animal is high-risk and unavailable for observation or testing
options.D: Whenever any household pet breaks the skin during playful activity

explanation: If a high-risk animal cannot be tested or watched for signs of rabies, we don't take chances—rabies prophylaxis is started right away.

question: How can you make sure your midwifery kit is always ready for an emergency call?

options.A: By washing the outside canvas bag once a year
options.B: By keeping the bag tightly locked until an emergency happens
options.C: By swapping metal tools for plastic toys to stay light
options.D: By checking inventory and expiry dates after every single use

explanation: Restocking and checking dates right after a case means you will never open your bag during an emergency only to find something expired or missing!

question: What was the main focus of early home care provided by ancient charitable groups?

options.A: Complex laboratory testing
options.B: Prescription drug management
options.C: Advanced surgical interventions
options.D: Basic hygiene, feeding, and comfort

explanation: Early home nursing was all about supportive care—keeping patients clean, well-fed, and comfortable rather than doing complex medical procedures.

question: What is a direct physical health risk when a widow drinks water used to wash a corpse?

options.A: Gastrointestinal infections from pathogens
options.B: Rapid development of bone mineral loss
options.C: Permanent damage to the optic nerve
options.D: Sudden onset of essential hypertension

explanation: Water that has touched a dead body carries harmful bacteria and viruses straight into the digestive system, causing serious tummy infections.

question: A community health nurse notices a sudden rush of parents requesting routine check-ups for young girls right before long school holidays. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Families preparing daughters for upcoming FGM ceremonies
options.B: Standard preventive screening recommended by public health
options.C: A sudden regional outbreak of adolescent infections
options.D: Parents seeking routine sports physicals for school teams

explanation: School holidays are prime time when families travel home or arrange for girls to undergo FGM. Always stay alert for these patterns in community practice!

question: For a couple under 35 years old, how long do they usually try to conceive through unprotected sex before doctors consider it infertility?

options.A: Twelve months or more
options.B: Three months or less
options.C: Six to nine months
options.D: At least two years

explanation: You've got this! Doctors look at a full 12 months of regular, unprotected sex as the standard timeline before testing for fertility issues. Keep up the great work!

question: Which muscle tissue type is under voluntary control?

options.A: Skeletal muscle
options.B: Visceral muscle
options.C: Cardiac muscle
options.D: Smooth muscle

explanation: Skeletal muscles attach to bones and allow conscious, voluntary control over body movements. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T12#GNS121_U3_T12_h1)

question: Which health model looks at wellness strictly as having no physical signs or symptoms of sickness?

options.A: Role performance model
options.B: Clinical model
options.C: Adaptive model
options.D: Eudaimonistic model

explanation: You've got this! The clinical model is the classic medical approach: if nothing hurts and you have no visible sickness, you are healthy.

question: Which of these is NOT a good strategy for helping a patient stick to a therapeutic diet long-term?

options.A: Involving family members in meal planning
options.B: Using herbs and spices to keep meals flavorful
options.C: Making gradual and sustainable food swaps
options.D: Making sudden, extreme food restrictions overnight without preparation

explanation: Going cold turkey on all your favorite foods overnight usually leads to burnout. Small, steady changes work best!

question: Where are interneurons found in the human body?

options.A: Along skeletal muscle fibers
options.B: Inside autonomic ganglia outside the spine
options.C: In peripheral skin receptors
options.D: Entirely within the central nervous system

explanation: Interneurons stay safely tucked away inside the brain and spinal cord, acting as the middlemen connecting sensory and motor pathways.

question: A common physical health complication for young girls forced into early marriage and childbearing is:

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.B: Type 2 diabetes
options.C: Obstetric fistula
options.D: Chronic kidney stones

explanation: The immature pelvis of a young girl combined with early childbirth frequently leads to severe birth injuries like obstetric fistula. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T10#GNS312_U1_T10_h3)

question: What financial headache do many NGOs face all the time?

options.A: Excessive government funding with no rules
options.B: Funding instability due to shifting donor priorities
options.C: Making too much profit from free clinics
options.D: Paying excessive taxes on humanitarian donations

explanation: Spot on! NGOs often worry about money because donors frequently change which regions or medical issues they choose to fund. [learn more](GNS124_U2_T6#GNS124_U2_T6_h5)

question: When taking off your personal protective equipment (PPE) after a procedure, which item should come off first?

options.A: Mask
options.B: Gloves
options.C: Eyewear
options.D: Gown

explanation: You got it! Gloves are usually the dirtiest item, so taking them off first stops you from spreading germs to your face or clothing.

question: If a patient's body has very low hormone levels for months, how will their target cells likely respond?

options.A: Receptor downregulation to conserve cellular energy
options.B: No change in receptor numbers on the cell membrane
options.C: Receptor upregulation to increase cellular sensitivity
options.D: Complete destruction of the hormone production glands

explanation: When hormones are scarce, cells put out more receptors—like putting out extra fishing nets—to catch every little bit of hormone that floats by. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h2)

question: Why does Lassa fever spike during the dry season?

options.A: Farming activities and bush burning drive rats closer to homes
options.B: Cold weather lowers human immune systems significantly
options.C: Increased humidity allows the virus to spread faster in the air
options.D: Heavy rainfall causes stagnant water to breed the virus

explanation: When fields are cleared and burned, the rats lose their natural habitat and move straight into grain stores and residential areas.

question: What is a common drawback of implementing MBO in a busy hospital?

options.A: It immediately stops all hospital equipment from breaking
options.B: It takes a lot of time away from direct patient care
options.C: It eliminates the need for physician consultations
options.D: It prevents nurses from working night shifts

explanation: The paperwork and meetings required for setting and reviewing goals can consume valuable time that might otherwise go to patient care. [learn more](GST321_U2_T4#GST321_U2_T4_h6)

question: How should you talk to a patient who has trouble hearing?

options.A: Shout loudly so the sound travels across the room
options.B: Whisper quietly directly into the patient's ear
options.C: Face the patient directly and speak in a normal tone
options.D: Use complex medical terms written on a notepad

explanation: Shouting actually distorts your words and makes lip-reading harder. Face them directly, speak clearly at a normal volume, and minimize background noise.

question: What is the main ethical focus of nursing care during the final stages of a degenerative disease?

options.A: Preserving patient dignity and providing comfort
options.B: Limiting family visits to reduce hospital noise and confusion
options.C: Forcing the patient to eat regular meals against their will
options.D: Finding experimental genetic treatments to reverse brain damage

explanation: You nailed it! When a disease reaches its end stage, the goal shifts from stopping the decline to ensuring comfort, pain relief, and deep dignity. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h7)

question: Which piece of information is NOT strictly required on a medication label immediately after dilution?

options.A: The exact dose and concentration prepared
options.B: The patient's favorite hobby or pastime
options.C: The generic or brand name of the drug
options.D: The initials of the nurse who mixed it

explanation: Personal hobbies are irrelevant to medication safety. Labels require identification of the drug, dose, patient, time, and preparer. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h6)

question: What is the biggest factor in whether a GPI patient will fully get their memory and thinking back after treatment?

options.A: How many family members live in their house
options.B: Catching and treating the disease early before permanent brain damage happens
options.C: The specific hospital ward they were admitted to
options.D: The patient's age when they were born

explanation: You nailed it! Antibiotics can kill the bacteria, but they cannot bring dead brain cells back to life. That's why early detection is everything!

question: What is the main job of a receptor in a reflex pathway?

options.A: Contraction of skeletal muscle fibers
options.B: Releasing hormones directly into the bloodstream
options.C: Converting physical stimuli into electrical nerve signals
options.D: Processing complex thoughts in the cerebral cortex

explanation: Receptors act like translators, changing physical stuff like heat or touch into the electrical language that nerves can understand.

question: Which behavioral change do we most often see in young children after experiencing a traumatic emergency?

options.A: Sudden independence and refusal of adult comfort
options.B: Complete emotional stability and mature coping
options.C: Advanced philosophical discussions about mortality
options.D: Behavioral regression like clinginess or bedwetting

explanation: Correct! Because little ones can't always put big stress into words, they often slide back to younger behaviors (regression) like clinging or bedwetting.

question: Why does your digestion temporarily slow down when you are suddenly startled or stressed?

options.A: The stomach stops working permanently due to shock
options.B: Food intake automatically increases during stressful times
options.C: Energy is diverted to muscles and vital organs for defense
options.D: Digestive enzymes turn into stress hormones instantly

explanation: Your body is smart! When danger hits, it pulls energy away from digesting food and sends it straight to your muscles so you can react fast.

question: What is the main goal of reproductive coercion in a relationship?

options.A: Promoting healthy spacing between all children in a community
options.B: Ensuring family planning clinics are adequately funded
options.C: Reducing overall maternal mortality rates in rural hospitals
options.D: Controlling a partner's reproductive outcomes to maintain power

explanation: Well done! Reproductive coercion involves tactics like tampering with birth control to force or block a pregnancy, keeping the victim trapped and dependent.

question: What is the primary goal of homeostasis in the human body?

options.A: Maintaining a stable internal environment
options.B: Speeding up cellular reproduction
options.C: Increasing muscle mass during exercise
options.D: Preventing all exposure to external bacteria

explanation: Homeostasis keeps vital internal conditions like temperature, blood pressure, and chemical balance within a safe, stable range. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which nursing action helps prevent joint stiffness (contractures) in a patient on bed rest?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to reduce swelling
options.B: Keeping the bed locked in a flat position all day
options.C: Performing range-of-motion exercises regularly
options.D: Applying ice packs to every major joint

explanation: Moving joints gently through their full range keeps muscles and tendons flexible and stops them from tightening up permanently.

question: What do we call a 'near miss' in the hospital?

options.A: An error that is caught before it reaches or harms the patient
options.B: A patient complaint about long waiting times at the clinic
options.C: A minor side effect of a drug that was expected by the doctor
options.D: An adverse event that causes permanent physical disability

explanation: Spot on! A near miss is a lucky save where a mistake almost happened, but someone caught it right on time before the patient got hurt.

question: What is a common myth among young people regarding Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)?

options.A: Regular screening helps catch hidden diseases
options.B: Condoms can help prevent transmission
options.C: People with STIs always look visibly sick
options.D: Some infections do not show early symptoms

explanation: Spot on! Many people are surprised to learn that numerous STIs show no early symptoms at all, meaning someone can feel completely healthy while carrying an infection.

question: What is the age range for adolescents according to the World Health Organization?

options.A: 5 to 12 years old
options.B: 18 to 25 years old
options.C: 10 to 19 years old
options.D: 13 to 30 years old

explanation: The World Health Organization specifically defines the adolescent bracket as spanning from age 10 through 19. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T1#GNS312_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the safest way to handle a deceased patient's jewelry and cash?

options.A: Document them and hand them to family or hospital administration
options.B: Send them along with the body directly to the mortuary
options.C: Give them to the ward cleaner for safekeeping
options.D: Leave them securely locked inside the bedside drawer

explanation: Valuables must be formally documented and given to the family or administrative authorities to prevent loss or theft. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T10#GNS221_U4_T10_h5)

question: What is the primary function of lysozyme found in tears?

options.A: Destroying bacteria
options.B: Refracting light rays
options.C: Lubricating the iris
options.D: Nourishing the cornea

explanation: Lysozyme is a natural antibacterial enzyme in tears that helps protect the eye surface from infection. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T1#GNS211_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why did Florence Nightingale place the most severely injured soldiers closest to the nurse's station?

options.A: To make it easier for doctors to perform sudden surgeries
options.B: To keep them away from noisy convalescing soldiers
options.C: To comply with strict military hierarchy rules
options.D: To allow for closer and more frequent observation

explanation: Placing the sickest patients near the nurses allowed staff to detect rapid changes in condition early. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h1)

question: What does setting a baseline mean in the context of community health planning?

options.A: Calculating the exact cost of building a fence around the clinic
options.B: Establishing the starting measurements to evaluate future progress
options.C: Writing down the names of all nurses working in the primary health center
options.D: Listing the minimum amount of salary a community health worker accepts

explanation: A baseline gives you initial numbers, like immunization coverage rates, so you can measure improvement after your program runs. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T6#GNS124_U3_T6_h2)

question: A private hospital hires someone to work as a nurse without checking their credentials, and the person ends up harming a patient. What type of hospital liability applies here?

options.A: Strict criminal liability
options.B: Corporate negligence
options.C: Immunity from prosecution
options.D: Vicarious liability only

explanation: Failing to check qualifications is a direct failure by the institution itself. That is a textbook example of corporate negligence!

question: A patient is admitted with suspected Neisseria meningitidis. What precautions should you start right away?

options.A: Reverse isolation to protect the patient from others
options.B: Standard precautions only with no masks needed
options.C: Strict airborne precautions in a negative pressure room
options.D: Droplet precautions

explanation: Neisseria meningitidis travels through respiratory droplets (talking, coughing, sneezing). Putting the patient on droplet precautions with a surgical mask protects everyone until the antibiotics kick in.

question: When a patient has vulval varicosities, which other body part should you check as a nurse?

options.A: The whites of the eyes
options.B: The lower extremities
options.C: The upper chest wall
options.D: The palms of the hands

explanation: Since pelvic congestion flows downward, it's very common to see leg varicose veins or swollen ankles accompanying vulval veins. Always look at the whole picture!

question: When a patient is suspected of having an unsafe abortion, what should be the primary goal of your first nursing assessment?

options.A: Identifying life-threatening complications and vital sign instability
options.B: Reporting the patient's family members to hospital authorities
options.C: Collecting evidence for police investigation and legal prosecution
options.D: Determining the exact herbal concoction ingested by the patient

explanation: In an emergency, airway, breathing, circulation, and watching for heavy bleeding or sepsis always come first. A nurse's duty is to save the patient's life, not play detective!

question: Which of these is NOT an environmental barrier to a nursing student's learning?

options.A: Extreme tiredness from a packed school timetable
options.B: Too much noise and overcrowded lecture halls
options.C: Helpful clinical preceptors and useful feedback
options.D: Not having enough basic medical training equipment

explanation: Supportive preceptors help you grow! Noise, shortages, and exhaustion are the real barriers that hold you back.

question: Which symptom is a major red flag for Meniere's disease?

options.A: Sudden complete ear pain
options.B: Bleeding from the ear canal
options.C: Purulent ear discharge
options.D: Episodic vertigo

explanation: Spot on! Meniere's disease causes sudden, severe spells of spinning dizziness (vertigo), along with ringing in the ears and hearing changes.

question: How is blood classified as a tissue in the human body?

options.A: Epithelial tissue
options.B: Nervous tissue
options.C: Muscular tissue
options.D: Connective tissue

explanation: You got this! Blood is a special type of connective tissue because it has living cells floating around in a fluid matrix called plasma. Think of it as a connecting transport system for the whole body.

question: Which chemical released in the body causes the rapid swelling and itching after an insect sting?

options.A: Amylase
options.B: Hemoglobin
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Histamine

explanation: Spot on! Venom triggers mast cells to release histamine, which makes local blood vessels open up and leak fluid into the skin, causing swelling and itchiness.

question: What happens to a mother's insulin requirements immediately after the placenta is delivered?

options.A: They increase sharply due to the stress of childbirth
options.B: They drop dramatically because placental hormones are gone
options.C: They fluctuate wildly for the first week postpartum
options.D: They remain exactly the same as during the third trimester

explanation: Once the placenta is out, the hormones that caused insulin resistance disappear, causing maternal insulin needs to fall sharply. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h7)

question: Why shouldn't you rush or speed too much when transporting an accident victim?

options.A: Vehicles consume too much fuel when driven too fast
options.B: Rushing can compromise the airway or worsen existing injuries
options.C: Hospitals prefer patients to arrive slowly for administrative reasons
options.D: Rescuers get too tired to document the incident properly

explanation: Spot on! Moving too fast without control can cause dropped stretchers or mess up breathing tubes. Smooth and steady wins the race in emergency care.

question: What are the three core parts of the epidemiological triangle used to study diseases?

options.A: Agent, host, and environment
options.B: Patient, nurse, and doctor
options.C: Bacteria, vaccine, and immunity
options.D: Clinic, hospital, and laboratory

explanation: Always remember the trio: the Agent (the germ), the Host (the person), and the Environment (where they meet). Simple and classic nursing knowledge!

question: What body regulates the Nurse Practice Act and professional standards for nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: Nigerian Medical and Dental Association
options.B: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
options.C: National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives
options.D: Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare

explanation: The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria is the statutory body charged with regulating nursing education and practice in the country. [learn more](GNS324_U2_T5#GNS324_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which major structural change happens in the lungs of someone with emphysema?

options.A: Thickening of the pleural space with fibrous scar tissue
options.B: Destruction of alveolar walls and loss of lung elasticity
options.C: Permanent blockage of the main pulmonary artery by clots
options.D: Excessive production of watery fluid inside the pleural cavity

explanation: You got it! Emphysema breaks down the walls of the air sacs and destroys the elastic fibers, making it hard for the lungs to bounce back when breathing out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h4)

question: Which sign is a key indicator of severe dehydration in a young child?

options.A: Bounding peripheral pulses
options.B: Lethargy or unconsciousness
options.C: Excessive tearing and crying
options.D: Eager drinking when offered a cup

explanation: When the body loses too much fluid and blood volume drops, the brain suffers, making the child very drowsy, limp, or unresponsive.

question: Why do we use a tiered, step-by-step system for healthcare delivery in Nigeria?

options.A: To make sure every health problem is handled at a teaching hospital
options.B: To restrict patient movement completely between rural and urban areas
options.C: To properly match the severity of health problems with the right facility
options.D: To ensure care is given based on how wealthy a patient is

explanation: Organizing care into tiers keeps things practical! Simple issues get solved right in the neighborhood, while complex cases go to well-equipped specialist centers.

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for making breast milk after childbirth?

options.A: Progesterone
options.B: Prolactin
options.C: Estrogen
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Pro-lactin promotes milk PRODUCTION. Remembering this trick makes exam questions a breeze!

question: A patient with psychomotor seizures has a history of a severe car accident two years ago. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Traumatic brain injury scarring
options.B: Degenerative autoimmune decline
options.C: Congenital metabolic defect
options.D: Primary brain tumor growth

explanation: Head injuries can disrupt brain pathways and leave scar tissue behind, which acts like a tiny spark plug for seizures later on. You are learning fast! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h2)

question: What should you do first if a smart bed's motorized controls stop working?

options.A: Submit a permanent replacement request to hospital administration
options.B: Check the power supply and ensure control lockouts are off
options.C: Immediately transfer the patient to a manual stretcher
options.D: Disassemble the mattress cover to check internal wiring

explanation: Always start with the simple stuff! Check if it's plugged in or if a safety lockout button was accidentally pressed.

question: How do nurses directly help with cancer epidemiology in clinical and community settings?

options.A: Funding public health research grants through private banks
options.B: Designing blueprints for modern oncology radiation bunkers
options.C: Manufacturing new chemotherapy drugs in hospital pharmacies
options.D: Accurate data collection and maintaining cancer registries

explanation: Nurses play a huge role by gathering precise patient data and keeping records updated, which helps researchers track cancer trends. You're making great progress! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: Why is smoking tobacco such a major risk factor for many types of cancer?

options.A: It introduces living cancer cells into the lungs
options.B: It blocks all major blood vessels
options.C: It contains harmful chemicals that damage cellular DNA
options.D: It stops red blood cells from forming

explanation: Tobacco smoke has active chemical carcinogens that mess up the genetic code inside healthy cells, triggering abnormal growth.

question: Why should you wipe away the very first drop of blood after a finger prick?

options.A: The first drop contains tissue fluid that dilutes the sample
options.B: The first drop has too many red blood cells
options.C: The first drop causes a meter error code
options.D: The first drop is full of dirt

explanation: Tissue fluid mixes into that very first drop and can make your glucose reading falsely low. Wiping it away gives you a clean sample!

question: Why do teenagers often take sudden risks without fully thinking things through?

options.A: They lack basic formal education regarding physical danger
options.B: The brain area for impulse control matures slower than the reward center
options.C: They have lower overall physical strength and poor balance
options.D: The visual cortex fails to judge speed and distance properly

explanation: Spot on! There is a developmental gap: the emotional reward center grows faster than the prefrontal cortex, which handles impulse control and long-term thinking.

question: How does pulling the neck bones back into alignment help the spinal canal?

options.A: Seal cerebrospinal fluid leaks inside the neck
options.B: Speed up the healing of torn skin tissues
options.C: Prevent the patient from developing a respiratory infection
options.D: Relieve pressure on the spinal cord by creating space

explanation: Great thinking. When the bones snap back into their correct spot, it opens up the spinal canal and takes dangerous pressure off the spinal cord.

question: Which finding is most commonly auscultated in the lungs of a patient experiencing fluid overload?

options.A: High-pitched whistling wheezes
options.B: Absent breath sounds on the left
options.C: A loud friction rub over the trachea
options.D: Fine crackles at the lung bases

explanation: Fluid backing up into the tiny air sacs of the lungs creates a crackling sound when air pops them open during inhalation. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which of these is a must-have element for any true community?

options.A: A modern tertiary care hospital within walking distance
options.B: A shared identity and feeling of belonging among people
options.C: A paved road network connecting all residential homes
options.D: An elected political representative in the national parliament

explanation: A community isn't just buildings and streets—it's the people! A shared sense of connection and belonging is what truly brings a community to life.

question: As a nurse, what is your absolute first priority when checking a patient who might have asphyxia?

options.A: Checking skin integrity over pressure points
options.B: Reviewing past medical and family history
options.C: Checking airway, breathing, and circulation
options.D: Measuring exact daily fluid intake and output

explanation: ABC comes first in every single emergency! Securing life-sustaining functions is always your top duty.

question: Prolonged pressure from the baby's head against the bladder during difficult labour can lead to which lasting complication?

options.A: Gestational hypertension
options.B: Vesicovaginal fistula
options.C: Chronic pelvic inflammatory disease
options.D: Placenta previa

explanation: This is a key one in midwifery practice. Continuous pressure cuts off blood flow to the bladder wall, forming an opening (fistula) that causes constant urine leakage.

question: What is the most common reason an unconscious adult lying flat on their back stops breathing well?

options.A: The tiny air sacs in the lungs collapse
options.B: Their tongue falls backward and blocks the throat
options.C: Thick mucus builds up in the windpipe
options.D: The bronchial tubes go into a sudden spasm

explanation: When someone passes out, their muscles relax completely. Gravity takes over, causing the lower jaw and tongue to slump backward and block the pharynx.

question: Why is teaming up with local community groups important for family care plans?

options.A: NGOs pay extra cash bonuses to community nurses
options.B: Local groups provide grassroots support and lasting assistance
options.C: Government laws make it illegal to work without church approval
options.D: International agencies handle all treatments for poor kids

explanation: Brilliant! Religious bodies, local cooperatives, and community groups offer friendly, ongoing support long after your nursing visit ends.

question: A family member wants to help their sibling remember daily HIV medications. What is a great first step?

options.A: Take the medication alongside the patient every single time
options.B: Wait until the patient misses three doses before speaking
options.C: Hide the medications in the kitchen to maintain privacy
options.D: Set daily phone alarms together to signal pill times

explanation: Smart thinking! Setting reliable phone alarms together is a practical way to build a steady daily routine for taking meds on time.

question: After a patient has an upper endoscopy, what is the most important nursing check before giving them water?

options.A: Administering a large meal immediately to test stomach tolerance
options.B: Checking for active bowel sounds every fifteen minutes
options.C: Keeping the patient flat on their back for at least six hours
options.D: Confirming that the patient's gag reflex has returned before offering fluids

explanation: Spot on! The throat spray numbs the back of the throat, so we must wait for the gag reflex to come back to prevent them from choking on water.

question: Why are asymptomatic carriers so tricky to deal with during disease outbreaks?

options.A: They develop severe complications that require immediate intensive care unit admission
options.B: They continue normal daily activities and spread the pathogen without knowing they are sick
options.C: They destroy the infection too quickly for laboratory tests to detect any antibodies
options.D: They carry mutated strains of bacteria that are completely immune to all known antibiotics

explanation: Because they don't feel sick, they don't stay home or isolate. They walk around living life normally while unintentionally passing the virus or bacteria along.

question: What is the biggest benefit of using simulation labs in nursing school?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for classroom lectures
options.B: Students can practice procedures safely before touching real patients
options.C: Students finish their training in half the standard time
options.D: It removes all clinical paperwork requirements

explanation: Well done! Sim labs give you a safe, stress-free zone to build your skills and confidence before working with real humans.

question: What is the safest tool for a nurse to use when measuring liquid medicine for an infant?

options.A: A regular dining cup
options.B: A standard kitchen teaspoon
options.C: A calibrated oral syringe
options.D: An intravenous syringe

explanation: Household spoons vary wildly in size! A calibrated oral syringe gives us the exact, pinpoint accuracy needed to keep tiny babies safe.

question: Why do women often lose bone density after reaching menopause?

options.A: High FSH destroys the bone marrow
options.B: Lower estrogen levels remove the protective effect on bones
options.C: The uterus stops making calcium
options.D: Lack of progesterone stops water absorption

explanation: Correct! Estrogen helps keep bones strong, so when it drops after menopause, the risk of weak bones (osteoporosis) goes up.

question: What is a key characteristic of direct ophthalmoscopy?

options.A: It produces an inverted image that must be flipped mentally
options.B: It requires a heavy head-mounted light source worn by the examiner
options.C: It provides an upright, magnified view of a small retinal area
options.D: It gives a complete wide-angle view of the entire peripheral retina

explanation: Direct ophthalmoscopy uses a handy device to give an upright image magnified roughly 15 times, though it covers a narrower field than indirect methods. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T8#GNS221_U2_T8_h3)

question: Which of these is a key responsibility of a nurse when caring for a suspected victim of violence?

options.A: Issuing formal protection orders to the abuser
options.B: Accurately documenting injuries and maintaining meticulous medical records
options.C: Acting as the presiding judge in court trials
options.D: Arresting the perpetrator at the hospital bedside

explanation: You nailed it! Clear and careful documentation by nurses serves as vital legal evidence in court to protect the patient.

question: Which item should be counted as part of a patient's fluid intake?

options.A: An intramuscular pain injection
options.B: An intravenous blood transfusion
options.C: A solid tablet pain medication
options.D: A dry solid piece of toast

explanation: Blood products and IV fluids introduce liquid directly into the vascular system and must be counted as intake. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h3)

question: Why do clinicians often use resting metabolic rate (RMR) instead of basal metabolic rate (BMR)?

options.A: It completely excludes the energy used by internal organs
options.B: It is always identical to total daily energy expenditure
options.C: It measures the exact calories burned during running
options.D: It requires fewer strict laboratory conditions to measure

explanation: Great job! RMR is much more practical in hospital and clinic settings because it doesn't force the patient to go through a strict 12-hour fast and absolute rest like BMR does.

question: How does the 'revolving' part of a DRF actually work in practice?

options.A: Unsold expired drugs are returned to manufacturers for full cash refunds
options.B: Donors inject new capital into the pharmacy every single month
options.C: Money collected from drug sales is used to buy fresh stock
options.D: Profits from drug sales are returned to the government treasury

explanation: Spot on! Patients buy drugs, that money goes back into the kitty, and the pharmacy uses it to buy the next batch. It is a continuous loop that keeps the pharmacy stocked.

question: Why is treating the root cause just as important as giving blood products when managing DIC?

options.A: The patient's kidneys will immediately filter out all infused platelets if they have a fever
options.B: The body will keep consuming clotting factors as long as the primary trigger remains active
options.C: Blood products will not work unless the patient's room temperature is carefully controlled
options.D: Transfusions can cause permanent damage to the liver if the infection is not cured first

explanation: Think of it like trying to bail water out of a leaking boat without fixing the hole. If you don't stop the infection or trauma causing the DIC, the body will just burn through your new blood products instantly.

question: How can you tell gestational hypertension apart from preeclampsia?

options.A: Gestational hypertension always starts before the 20th week.
options.B: Gestational hypertension includes seizures while preeclampsia does not.
options.C: Gestational hypertension permanently damages the kidneys.
options.D: Gestational hypertension does not involve protein in the urine or organ damage.

explanation: Both conditions bring high BP after 20 weeks, but preeclampsia is unique because it causes protein to leak into the urine or stresses other body organs.

question: Which of these does NOT help cause a disease outbreak?

options.A: High routine immunization coverage in children
options.B: Inadequate waste management systems
options.C: Poor access to safe, clean drinking water
options.D: Overcrowded housing and living quarters

explanation: Vaccines are our shield! High immunization rates protect a community and stop outbreaks, unlike bad water or crowded living spaces which spread disease.

question: What do 'determinants' represent in epidemiological studies?

options.A: The administrative rules governing public health nurses
options.B: The financial cost of treating a chronic illness in a clinic
options.C: The causes and risk factors that influence health and disease
options.D: The total number of hospital beds available in a community

explanation: Don't let the big word trip you up! Determinants are simply the underlying causes and risk factors—like germs, habits, or surroundings—that change someone's health status.

question: What does the psychosocial dimension in palliative care primarily focus on?

options.A: Surgical correction of terminal organs
options.B: Emotional, social, and psychological needs
options.C: Nutritional intake and calorie counting
options.D: Strict measurement of vital signs

explanation: Psychosocial care deals with the mental, emotional, and social well-being of the patient rather than purely physical functions. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T16#GNS321_U4_T16_h1)

question: A nurse is preparing to feed a patient via a PEG tube. What action should be performed first?

options.A: Flush the tube rapidly with 100 mL of cold water
options.B: Lie the patient completely flat to check the abdomen
options.C: Verify tube placement and assess bowel sounds
options.D: Attach the feeding bag and start the pump immediately

explanation: Safety checks like confirming tube position and ensuring active bowel sounds must always happen before introducing any fluid or formula. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h3)

question: How do mass movements differ from regular mixing movements in the large intestine?

options.A: Segmental movements require conscious effort to move waste.
options.B: Segmental contractions happen only once or twice a day.
options.C: Mass movements push stool a long way toward the rectum all at once.
options.D: Mass movements happen non-stop all day and night.

explanation: Mass movements are like big, powerful waves that sweep through the colon every now and then to clear out stored waste toward the exit. You've got this!

question: Why is setting up a large IV line so important for an anaemic woman in labor?

options.A: To give oral drugs straight into her veins
options.B: To keep track of her internal body temperature
options.C: To quickly give blood or IV fluids if heavy bleeding starts
options.D: To stop gestational diabetes

explanation: A good, wide cannula is a lifesaver—it lets you pump in blood or fluids instantly if postpartum bleeding happens.

question: A patient comes in with a metal flake stuck on the surface of their eye. Why is irrigation a good choice here?

options.A: Fluid pressure forces the metal deeper to hide the pain
options.B: Washing the eye replaces the need for a physical eye exam
options.C: Irrigation completely dissolves metal on contact
options.D: The fluid stream can safely flush away loose surface irritants

explanation: Spot on! If something is just resting loosely on the surface, a gentle, steady flow of liquid is a safe way to float it right out.

question: What is a primary assessment tool used during a home prenatal visit to check fetal well-being?

options.A: Peak flow meter
options.B: Digital thermometer
options.C: Doppler device
options.D: Glucometer strip

explanation: A portable Doppler is used during home visits to listen to the fetal heart rate and confirm fetal viability. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T13#GNS324_U3_T13_h3)

question: How is pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) affecting the Fallopian tubes primarily treated in a stable patient?

options.A: Continuous peritoneal dialysis
options.B: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.C: Immediate emergency surgery
options.D: Radiation therapy

explanation: You're crushing it. Because PID is an infection, the frontline treatment is medical—hitting it hard with the right antibiotics to clear the bacteria.

question: Who has the main responsibility for setting health rules that must be followed in a school?

options.A: The local police department
options.B: Enrolling students
options.C: Parent-teacher athletics committees
options.D: School management

explanation: Exactly! The school management team holds the authority required to create and enforce official health policies.

question: Why would a doctor order a hypotonic fluid like 0.45% Normal Saline?

options.A: To maintain a stable vein without altering any fluid balance
options.B: To rapidly replace large volumes of blood loss from trauma
options.C: To treat severe cellular dehydration by moving water into tissues
options.D: To pull excess fluid out of swollen brain cells and tissues

explanation: Think of hypotonic fluids as having fewer particles than blood. When a patient is super dehydrated, these fluids move out of the veins and into thirsty cells to plump them back up!

question: In the context of vulnerable families, what is 'property grabbing'?

options.A: Community members stealing food donations meant for orphans
options.B: Relatives seizing land and belongings after a parent dies
options.C: The government confiscating hospital records of deceased patients
options.D: Banks freezing accounts belonging to children under age eighteen

explanation: Property grabbing happens when greedy relatives unlawfully chase away a grieving widow and her children to take over their home and properties. It's a harsh reality nurses should be aware of to guide families.

question: What is the main reason health risks must be prioritized after an assessment?

options.A: Resources and funds are always limited
options.B: The government bans solving more than one problem
options.C: Nurses are not allowed to address environmental problems
options.D: Communities never suffer from more than two health issues

explanation: We would love to fix every single problem at once, but money and time are always limited. Prioritizing helps us tackle the most urgent issues first.

question: What is the main difference between a standard IV infusion and a blood transfusion?

options.A: Transfusions never require a special intravenous line
options.B: Infusions are always given faster than blood transfusions
options.C: Infusions can only use blood products while transfusions use plain water
options.D: Infusions deliver fluids or medications while transfusions replace blood components

explanation: You've got this! Regular IV fluids give water, salts, or drugs, while blood transfusions specifically replace parts of the blood like red cells or plasma. Simple and clear!

question: What does an electroencephalography (EEG) test actually measure?

options.A: Oxygen saturation levels in brain tissue
options.B: Intracranial pressure inside the skull
options.C: Electrical activity of the brain
options.D: Blood flow velocity in brain vessels

explanation: Think of an EEG like a smart sensor that picks up the tiny electrical signals your brain cells make as they talk to each other! It's a great, painless way to see how the brain is functioning.

question: Which quick physical check is critical before prescribing a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive?

options.A: Chest X-ray imaging
options.B: Fasting blood glucose test
options.C: Blood pressure measurement
options.D: Routine eye examination

explanation: Always check the BP first! Estrogen can sometimes cause blood pressure to rise or increase clot risks, so checking baseline BP keeps your client safe.

question: How does the medication hydroxyurea help treat sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: It increases the production of foetal haemoglobin
options.B: It binds directly to iron stores to prevent liver damage
options.C: It destroys white blood cells to prevent chronic inflammation
options.D: It dilates peripheral blood vessels to lower blood pressure

explanation: Hydroxyurea is a fantastic drug for this condition. It tricks the body into making more foetal haemoglobin, which stops haemoglobin S from clumping together and prevents cells from sickling.

question: In nursing, what is the golden rule regarding documentation?

options.A: It cost no money to execute
options.B: It legally never happened
options.C: It was performed perfectly
options.D: It was done by a doctor instead

explanation: Remember this rule always! Courts and professional boards only trust written notes. If it's not documented, legally, it was never done.

question: In maternal health, what does the 'second delay' usually involve?

options.A: Delays by the government in building enough clinics in urban areas
options.B: Delays by doctors in prescribing the correct antibiotics during labor
options.C: Delays in the manufacturing of essential maternity drugs and supplies
options.D: Delays in reaching a medical facility due to transportation or household power dynamics

explanation: The second delay is all about the journey to the hospital. It drags out when a pregnant woman has to wait for transport money or permission from family members.

question: How should a nurse respond when a patient talks about a frightening delusion?

options.A: Tell the client that police are on their way to arrest them
options.B: Argue aggressively until the client admits the belief is false
options.C: Acknowledge the emotional distress without validating the false belief
options.D: Ignore the statement completely and change the subject

explanation: Well done! Show empathy for how scary the feeling is, but don't agree with the unreal belief. It keeps trust strong!

question: What happens directly when a patient with a chronic illness stops taking their medications?

options.A: Immediate complete cure of the condition
options.B: Permanent immunity from future infections
options.C: Disease progression and frequent relapses
options.D: Automatic stabilization of vital signs

explanation: Without steady medication levels in the body, chronic conditions flare up and lead to new health crises.

question: What does the term 'intervention fidelity' mean in community nursing?

options.A: Delivering the program activities exactly as they were designed
options.B: Writing accurate monthly financial expenditure reports
options.C: Ensuring community members trust the local nursing staff
options.D: Securing loyal financial donors for long-term health projects

explanation: Fidelity simply means sticking to the script! It's about carrying out the health program just the way it was planned to work best.

question: What is the primary digestive function of the oral cavity?

options.A: Absorption of complex carbohydrates into the bloodstream
options.B: Production of powerful hydrochloric acid to sterilize food
options.C: Complete enzymatic breakdown and absorption of proteins
options.D: Mechanical breakdown of food and mixing it with saliva

explanation: The mouth starts digestion by chewing food into smaller pieces and mixing it with saliva to create an easy-to-swallow bolus. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T1#GNS121_U1_T1_h1)

question: What is the main superpower of community herd immunity?

options.A: Reducing the cost of hospital building construction
options.B: Protecting vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated
options.C: Eliminating the need for clean water and sanitation
options.D: Ensuring every adult receives an annual booster shot

explanation: When most people around are immunized, it builds a protective shield around babies or sick individuals who cannot take vaccines yet. Brilliant concept to master!

question: What is an advantage of using indirect methods like pill counts over direct laboratory tests?

options.A: They require expensive laboratory equipment and blood draws
options.B: They completely eliminate the possibility of human error
options.C: They are practical, affordable, and easy to use in routine clinic visits
options.D: They measure exact chemical concentrations inside the patient's liver

explanation: Indirect methods like pill counts and patient interviews are low-cost, non-invasive, and easily integrated into everyday nursing assessments. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h4)

question: In a patient health history, what do we mean by the 'chief complaint'?

options.A: The primary reason the patient is seeking care, in their own words
options.B: The surgical history from the patient's childhood
options.C: The final medical diagnosis written by the attending physician
options.D: A complete list of every prescription medication the patient takes

explanation: Spot-on! The chief complaint is simply the main trouble or symptom that brought the patient to the clinic, written using what they tell you.

question: You notice low-income women at the antenatal clinic aren't getting family planning info. What is the best advocacy action?

options.A: Working with the team to set up clear education sessions for all patients
options.B: Telling the affected patients to find a different hospital on their own
options.C: Ignoring the issue because it's not bedside nursing work
options.D: Reporting the patients to hospital management for asking questions

explanation: Good advocacy means speaking up and working with your team to make sure every single patient gets equal access to health information. Great job! [learn more](GNS216_U1_T8#GNS216_U1_T8_h9)

question: Why do working nurses need continuous professional development (CPD) programs?

options.A: Nursing councils require staff to sit for weekly written exams
options.B: It is the only way to prevent nurses from resigning from the job
options.C: Hospital management needs a way to reduce staff salary budgets
options.D: Medical knowledge and clinical technology change over time

explanation: Medicine never stays still! CPD helps nurses stay updated with new life-saving techniques, equipment, and medical knowledge throughout their careers.

question: What is the specific name of the stress ulcer that forms in the stomach due to severe burn trauma?

options.A: Zollinger-Ellison ulcer
options.B: Cushing's ulcer
options.C: Peptic ulcer
options.D: Curling's ulcer
